query: How can relax-and-fix be integrated with L-shaped/Benders decomposition, and under what conditions do they complement or conflict?

response.query: How can relax-and-fix be integrated with L-shaped/Benders decomposition, and under what conditions do they complement or conflict?
response.answer: Relax-and-fix can complement L-shaped/Benders decomposition by providing initial feasible solutions and accelerating convergence. They conflict when both methods generate conflicting cuts or solutions. Use them together for complex, multistage optimization problems.

results.title: The Benders decomposition algorithm: A literature review - ScienceDirect
results.content:
Title: The Benders decomposition algorithm: A literature review - ScienceDirect
The Benders decomposition algorithm has been successfully applied to a wide range of difficult optimization problems. We also discuss the use of the Benders Decomposition to develop efficient (meta-)heuristics, describe the limitations of the classical algorithm, and present extensions enabling its application to a broader range of problems. It has been more than five decades since the *Benders Decomposition* (*BD*) algorithm was proposed by Benders (1962), with the main objective of tackling problems with *complicating variables,* which, when temporarily fixed, yield a problem significantly easier to handle. Hence, one solves the equivalent model by applying a relaxation strategy to the feasibility and optimality cuts, yielding a *Master Problem* (*MP*) and a subproblem, which are iteratively solved to respectively guide the search process and generate the violated cuts. The main goal of this paper therefore is to contribute to filling this gap by reviewing the current state-of-the-art, focusing on the main ideas for accelerating the method, discussing the main variants and extensions aimed to handle more general problems involving, e.g., nonlinear/integer/constraint programming subproblems, and identifying trends and promising research directions. We propose a taxonomy of the enhancement and acceleration strategies based on the main components of the algorithm: the decomposition strategy, the strategies to handle the MP and subproblem, and the strategies to generate solutions and cuts. ### An improved Benders decomposition algorithm for the tree of hubs location problem. ### Benders decomposition for discrete–continuous linear bilevel problems with application to traffic network design. ### Decomposition techniques for multistage scheduling problems using mixed-integer and constraint programming methods. ### Solving multistage quantified linear optimization problems with the alpha–beta nested Benders decomposition. ### A computational study of Benders decomposition for the integrated aircraft routing and crew scheduling problem. ### Accelerating Benders decomposition with heuristic master problem solutions. There are general decomposition approaches for specific problems, such as the L-Shaped algorithm [155] or Benders Decomposition [156]. The column-and-constraint generation method and Benders decomposition are used to solve the two models, and a thorough comparison among the deterministic facility location problem with drones (FLPD) models and three proposed models are also presented. To solve this computationally challenging stochastic optimization model, we employ an exact Benders decomposition-based branch-and-cut algorithm.

results.title: Automatic Benders’ Decomposition — AIMMS How-To
results.content:
Title: Automatic Benders’ Decomposition — AIMMS How-To
# Automatic Benders’ Decomposition. Benders’ decomposition is an approach to solve complicated mathematical programming problems by splitting them into two, and thereby simplifying the solution process by (repeatedly) solving one master problem and one subproblem. If the problem contains integer variables then typically they become part of the master problem while the continuous variables become part of the subproblem. The classic approach of the Benders’ decomposition algorithm solves an alternating sequence of master problems and subproblems. Benders’ decomposition is mostly used for solving difficult MIP problems and stochastic programming problems. We have developed a generic Benders’ decomposition module in AIMMS that is easy to use. The Benders’ decomposition module in AIMMS is implemented as an open algorithm using GMP functionality. Besides the classic approach the module contains a modern variant that solves one master (MIP) problem using solver callbacks. (See also Paul Rubin’s blog post Benders Decomposition Then and Now.). To use Benders’ decomposition, first install the system module `GMPBendersDecomposition`. To solve a MIP problem using the classic approach you can use the following:. 1! First we must generate the GMP for our Math Program. The second argument defines the master problem variables. The third argument (`'Classic'`) of the above procedure specifies the algorithm that will be used. The two-phase algorithm solves a relaxed problem in the first phase and the original MIP problem in the second phase (using either the classic or modern approach). The current implementation of Benders’ decomposition in AIMMS has some limitations. It cannot be used to solve nonlinear problems. Also, the current implementation does not support multiple subproblems which could be efficient in case the subproblem has a block diagonal structure. This implies that the current implementation cannot be used to solve (two stage) stochastic programming problems with a subproblem for each scenario.
